text_blocks.snippet: While self breast exams are no longer widely recommended as a primary screening method for breast cancer, the concept of breast awareness is still important. This means knowing how your breasts normally look and feel, and reporting any changes to a healthcare provider, according to the American Cancer Society.
snippet_highlighted_words: self breast exams are no longer widely recommended as a primary screening method for breast cancer

list.title: Why the change?
list.snippet: Research has not shown that regular breast self-exams reduce deaths from breast cancer, and they can lead to unnecessary worry and procedures due to false positives.

list.title: Breast awareness is key:
list.snippet: Instead of a formal monthly exam, focus on knowing your breasts and reporting any new changes (lumps, skin changes, nipple discharge, etc.) to your doctor.

list.title: When to see a doctor:
list.snippet: If you notice any of the following changes, it's important to contact your healthcare provider immediately: a lump, skin irritation, dimpling or puckering of the skin, nipple retraction, redness or swelling, or nipple discharge according to RWJBarnabas Health.

list.title: Mammograms are the primary screening tool:
list.snippet: For women at average risk, mammograms are recommended starting at age 40, with regular screenings (every other year) as the primary method for detecting breast cancer early according to the University of Rochester Medical Center.

list.title: Consult your doctor:
list.snippet: If you have any concerns about breast health, or if you would like to discuss breast self-exams further, it is best to consult with your doctor or other healthcare provider, says the American Cancer Society.
